overview: 829 Ocean Park Blvd is a seven-unit, two-story apartment building on the northeast corner of Ocean Park Blvd and 9th St in the Sunset Park neighborhood of Santa Monica. The county carries the building at 5,682 SF on a 6,603 SF lot, built 1953 with an effective year of 1959, under zoning code SMR3A. Title has not changed hands in a market sale since the 1975 base year; the recorded transfers since then are a spousal transfer, a trust transfer and a file correction.

The February 27, 2026 rent roll shows all seven units occupied at $1,711.73 to $3,000 per month, $17,107.19 in total. Leasing history supports a mix of one and two bedrooms; the analysis carries four two bedrooms and three one bedrooms pending ownership's confirmation. The building has an on-site laundry room that produced about $100 per month, storage, gas ranges, hardwood floors and non-assigned parking at the rear.

At the recommended $2.45M the property prices at $350,000 per unit and $431 per SF, a 5.24% return on current income and 6.51% at underwritten market rents. The closed Sunset Park sales of the past fourteen months ran $310,000 to $458,000 per unit and $367 to $528 per SF at cap rates of 5.00% to 6.07%, and the sale directly behind the subject on Maple St closed at 5.87%. The subject prices inside every range and below the Maple St yield because its income has more room to grow.
properties.location_title: Sunset Park, Santa Monica, One Mile From Main Street and the Sand
location_narrative: The property sits at the corner of Ocean Park Blvd and 9th St, between Lincoln Blvd and the Ocean Park neighborhood, in the 90405 ZIP code. Ocean Park Blvd runs west to Main Street and the beach in about a mile and east to Santa Monica College and the Expo Line's 17th Street station. Lincoln Blvd, one block west, carries the retail corridor from Rose Avenue to downtown Santa Monica, and Whole Foods, Trader Joe's and Santa Monica Airport Park are all within ten minutes.

The 90405 ZIP code reports 27,298 residents with a median age of 43.1 and a median household income of $121,241, and 69% of its households rent. Median gross rent is $2,417. The parcel scores 87 on Walk Score, 57 on Transit Score and 88 on Bike Score, and sits in FEMA Zone X, an area of minimal flood hazard. HUD's 2026 small-area fair market rents for the ZIP are $2,850 for a one bedroom and $3,550 for a two bedroom.

Sunset Park is one of the few Westside submarkets where small buildings still trade in volume: nine five to twelve unit sales closed in the ZIP between June 2025 and August 2026, including one on the subject's own block. Buyers here are choosing among 1930s to 1970s walk-ups at similar yields, which is why the evidence for this pricing is direct rather than inferred from other neighborhoods.
physical_narrative: The building is a two-story wood-frame and stucco structure of 5,682 SF on a 6,603 SF corner lot, built 1953. The street elevation on Ocean Park Blvd carries a decorative wrought-iron screen, a flagstone planter and a lawn; the 9th St side holds the exterior stair and the gated parking area at the rear. The county records seven units and no per-unit areas.

Leasing history describes the units as one and two bedrooms with gas ranges, hardwood floors and, in the units turned most recently, new paint, new kitchens and remodeled baths; one two bedroom was advertised at 850 SF with central air. The building has a common laundry room, storage space and non-assigned on-site parking with one space offered per unit. Unit square footages are not published by the county or ownership and are omitted from this analysis.

A 1953 building under one family's ownership for fifty years will be underwritten by buyers on what has not been done as much as what has. Ownership's schedule shows a well-run building with modest bills, but it is one month of expenses rather than a year, and the seismic retrofit status, roof, plumbing and electrical service should be documented before launch. This analysis carries repairs at $800 per unit and reserves at $250 per unit rather than the owner's actual cost.
market_narrative: Nine closed sales of five to twelve unit buildings in 90405 since June 2025 frame the subject. The five to seven unit sales closed at $2,170,000 to $2,525,000, and where income was reported, at cap rates of 5.00% to 6.07% and multipliers of 11.58 to 12.89. The two most instructive are 824 Maple St, directly behind the subject, at $2,525,000 and a 5.87% cap in May 2026, and 2332 20th St, a 1959 six-unit of similar mix, at $2,210,000 and a 6.07% cap in July 2026.

The active listings are the other half of the picture. 2648 23rd St, an eight-unit 1949 building with the same one and two bedroom mix and seven renovated units, asks $3.2M at a published 5.50% cap. 1937 17th St, a six-unit 1948 building with two vacancies, asks $2.25M at 5.00%. The subject at $2.45M sits between them on price, below both on price per square foot, and offers a fully occupied roll that neither does.
positioning_narrative: The right buyer values what is scarce here: a corner lot a mile from the beach, seven paying tenants, a clean title history and two units whose rents reset on turnover. That buyer should be qualified early on whether they will hold for the turnover or want it priced in, because the answer decides whether an offer lands at the top or the bottom of the range.
rent_narrative: Rent evidence is read plan by plan. Seven one-bedroom listings in Sunset Park run $2,190 to $2,900 and average $2,591, with the two on Ocean Park Blvd at $2,875 and $2,900 and an unrenovated 700 SF unit two blocks away at $2,190. Eight two-bedroom listings run $2,795 to $3,800 and average $3,154; the 850 to 908 SF units with published area ask $2,800 to $2,895, and a renovated two bedroom one block south on Hill St asks $3,450.

The market column carries $2,500 for the one bedrooms and $3,100 for the two bedrooms, below the listing averages and below HUD's 2026 fair market rents for the ZIP. The subject's most recent leases at $2,550 and $2,795 to $3,000 confirm the two-bedroom figure is achievable without renovation. The gap between the current and market columns is $2,793 per month, and about $1,500 of it sits in the two long-term one-bedroom tenancies, which under Santa Monica rent control recover only when those tenants choose to leave.
valuation_narrative: The recommended list price is $2.45M, inside an opinion-of-value range of $2.35M to $2.55M. Current scheduled income of $205,286 less a 3% vacancy reserve plus $1,197 of laundry income gives $200,325 of effective gross income; operating expenses of $71,998, including taxes reassessed at the list price, produce net operating income of $128,327, a 5.24% cap rate and an 11.93 gross rent multiplier. At underwritten market rents of $238,800 the net operating income is $159,535 and the cap rate 6.51%. The price is $350,000 per unit and $431 per SF.

Against the evidence, the price is disciplined. It sits inside the closed per-unit range, inside the closed per-square-foot range, at a yield between the 5.00% Pacific St sale and the 5.87% Maple St sale, and at a multiplier between Maple and 20th Street. The reasons it is not higher are the same reasons it is defensible: two units 30% under market that recover only on turnover, a one-month expense record, and a 1953 building whose retrofit status is not yet documented. A buyer who underwrites the turnover will pay the top of the range; a buyer who prices it out will pay the bottom.

strategy.title: Price Off the Sale Behind the Building
strategy.copy: 824 Maple St shares the block with the subject and closed in May 2026 at $2,525,000, a 5.87% cap and an 11.58 multiplier. Every buyer who tours will know that sale. Pricing at $2.45M, a 5.24% cap and an 11.93 multiplier on a smaller building with more rent upside sits deliberately in the shadow of that print rather than above it, and the offering should say so rather than let a buyer discover it.

strategy.title: Sell the Turnover Story Honestly
strategy.copy: Two of the seven units rent at $1,712 and $1,757 against a one-bedroom market of about $2,500. That is roughly $1,500 per month of income that arrives only when those tenants leave, and no one can promise when. The offering should show the current column and the market column side by side, state that the gap is turnover-dependent under Santa Monica rent control, and let the buyer price the timing. Buyers who find that gap on their own treat it as a problem; buyers who are shown it treat it as the reason to buy.

strategy.title: Have the Registry and the Bills Ready Before Launch
strategy.copy: The documents a Santa Monica buyer asks for on the first call are the Rent Control Board registration for each unit, twelve months of bills, and the seismic retrofit status. Ownership has provided a rent roll and one month of expenses. Assembling the registry printout, a trailing statement and the City's retrofit letter before launch removes the three questions that stall escrows on buildings of this vintage.

buyer_profiles.title: Westside Small-Building Owner
buyer_profiles.copy: Owners who already hold five to fifteen unit buildings in Santa Monica, Venice and Mar Vista, including the buyers on the Maple, 20th Street and Grant Street sales this year. They know the registry, the General Adjustment and the tenant base, and they buy on yield against a known turnover path.

buyer_profiles.title: 1031 Exchange Buyer
buyer_profiles.copy: Sellers trading out of larger or more management-intensive assets into a Westside replacement property under a 45-day identification clock. The 2332 20th St buyer in July was completing an exchange, and a fully occupied Santa Monica corner building at a 5.24% yield is exactly the identification that pool makes.

buyer_profiles.title: Long-Hold Family Investor
buyer_profiles.copy: Families and individuals who buy Santa Monica apartments to hold for decades, the same profile as the current ownership. They pay for location and tenant stability rather than the first-year yield, and they are the buyers most likely to reach the top of the range.

rent_control.conclusion: The building was completed in 1953 and is subject to the City of Santa Monica Rent Control Charter Amendment, which covers residential rental units with certificates of occupancy before April 10, 1979. Each unit carries a registered Maximum Allowable Rent that may rise by the Rent Control Board's annual General Adjustment, 2.6% with a $70 cap for September 1, 2026. Under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act a unit re-rents at market when a tenant leaves voluntarily and that rent becomes the new base; the pro forma in this analysis assumes re-rent at market on turnover only. Registration status and the current Maximum Allowable Rent for each unit should be confirmed with the Rent Control Board before marketing.

zoning.conclusion: The assessor carries the parcel under zoning code SMR3A, the City of Santa Monica's R3 Medium Density Residential district, on a 6,603 SF corner lot. The property is presented as built: a two-story seven-unit apartment building with on-site parking. No entitlement or development scenario is relied upon; a buyer should verify the zoning designation and any nonconforming status with the City of Santa Monica Planning Division.

development.conclusion: No development scenario is relied upon in this valuation. The property is valued as an operating seven-unit apartment building.

The property sits at the corner of Ocean Park Blvd and 9th St, between Lincoln Blvd and the Ocean Park neighborhood, in the 90405 ZIP code. Ocean Park Blvd runs west to Main Street and the beach in about a mile and east to Santa Monica College and the Expo Line's 17th Street station. Lincoln Blvd, one block west, carries the retail corridor from Rose Avenue to downtown Santa Monica, and Whole Foods, Trader Joe's and Santa Monica Airport Park are all within ten minutes.

The 90405 ZIP code reports 27,298 residents with a median age of 43.1 and a median household income of $121,241, and 69% of its households rent. Median gross rent is $2,417. The parcel scores 87 on Walk Score, 57 on Transit Score and 88 on Bike Score, and sits in FEMA Zone X, an area of minimal flood hazard. HUD's 2026 small-area fair market rents for the ZIP are $2,850 for a one bedroom and $3,550 for a two bedroom.

Sunset Park is one of the few Westside submarkets where small buildings still trade in volume: nine five to twelve unit sales closed in the ZIP between June 2025 and August 2026, including one on the subject's own block. Buyers here are choosing among 1930s to 1970s walk-ups at similar yields, which is why the evidence for this pricing is direct rather than inferred from other neighborhoods.

The building is a two-story wood-frame and stucco structure of 5,682 SF on a 6,603 SF corner lot, built 1953. The street elevation on Ocean Park Blvd carries a decorative wrought-iron screen, a flagstone planter and a lawn; the 9th St side holds the exterior stair and the gated parking area at the rear. The county records seven units and no per-unit areas.

Leasing history describes the units as one and two bedrooms with gas ranges, hardwood floors and, in the units turned most recently, new paint, new kitchens and remodeled baths; one two bedroom was advertised at 850 SF with central air. The building has a common laundry room, storage space and non-assigned on-site parking with one space offered per unit. Families and individuals who buy Santa Monica apartments to hold for decades, the same profile as the current ownership. They pay for location and tenant stability rather than the first-year yield, and they are the buyers most likely to reach the top of the range.

rent_control.conclusion: The building was completed in 1953 and is subject to the City of Santa Monica Rent Control Charter Amendment, which covers residential rental units with certificates of occupancy before April 10, 1979. Each unit carries a registered Maximum Allowable Rent that may rise by the Rent Control Board's annual General Adjustment, 2.6% with a $70 cap for September 1, 2026. Under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act a unit re-rents at market when a tenant leaves voluntarily and that rent becomes the new base; the pro forma in this analysis assumes re-rent at market on turnover only. Registration status and the current Maximum Allowable Rent for each unit should be confirmed with the Rent Control Board before marketing.

zoning.conclusion: The assessor carries the parcel under zoning code SMR3A, the City of Santa Monica's R3 Medium Density Residential district, on a 6,603 SF corner lot. The property is presented as built: a two-story seven-unit apartment building with on-site parking. No entitlement or development scenario is relied upon; a buyer should verify the zoning designation and any nonconforming status with the City of Santa Monica Planning Division.
